key_takeaways: The GovAI Coalition (founded by San Jose, Nov 2023; 150+ member governments) publishes the most directly reusable artifacts: a 22-field AI FactSheet vendor questionnaire (an 'AI nutrition label' inspired by IBM's FactSheets 360), a separate FactSheet for service providers, and a 4-page Vendor Agreement contract addendum with 14 enforceable requirements — all free at sanjoseca.gov (which blocks scripted fetchers; use mirrors like cfsa.dc.gov or a reader proxy).

The GovAI Vendor Agreement's core asks recur everywhere and should anchor the wizard: NIST-AI-RMF/ISO-42001 risk plan on request, AI incident investigation with 30-day cure, agency data ownership, free machine-readable data export, performance-monitoring means (FPR/FNR/error rates), bias-management evidence, human override of all outputs, explainability, end-user notice, staff training, and no-cost audit rights.

OMB rescinded M-24-10/M-24-18 in April 2025; the current federal stack is M-25-21 (use/governance) + M-25-22 (acquisition, applies to solicitations after ~Sept 30, 2025) + M-26-04 (Dec 11, 2025, LLM 'Unbiased AI' transparency). Cite these, not the 2024 memos.

M-25-22's contract terms are the best model anti-lock-in language: permanent ban on training public models with non-public government data absent consent, data/model portability, agency-held test data the vendor cannot see, independent evaluation rights, no gag clauses on test results, version rollback rights, and new-AI-feature notification; footnote 25 gives evaluable pro-competition vendor practices including uniform public pricing and subcontractor disclosure.

M-26-04 defines a concrete two-tier LLM documentation demand: minimum (acceptable use policy; model/system/data cards; end-user resources; feedback mechanism) and enhanced (system prompts, content-moderation categories, red-teaming, bias-eval methodology and benchmarks, non-US training/development disclosure, and reseller-added modifications) — with materiality language supporting termination for default.

M-25-21 presumes benefits-agency use cases are high-impact AI (eligibility determination, continued-eligibility, benefits-access biometrics, fraud detection, decision-informing translation) and prescribes minimum practices (pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, monitoring, training, human oversight/fail-safe, appeals, public feedback) — the wizard should auto-escalate its question tier when a pitch matches these, which are exactly the top categories in the 2026 New America benefits survey.

California is the most operationalized state system: EO N-12-23 → mandatory GenAI disclosure language in ALL solicitations → STD 1000 vendor factsheet (retired Feb 2025) → GenAI terms now embedded in standard model contracts (PD 401 §16, PD 402/403 §22, Rev. 2/20/25) → SIMM 5305-F risk assessment plus the streamlined SIMM 150 (Sept 2025), which asks vendors for model+version, license tier, and delivery model, and rates resident-facing chatbots and eligibility assessments at least Moderate risk.

Washington's DATA-04 policy (Dec 11, 2025) contains the cleanest single diligence item: vendors of high-risk GenAI must certify an AI governance program consistent with NIST AI RMF; it also requires data-sharing agreements restricting model training on agency data, high-risk adoption plans with environmental impacts and opt-out rights, and bans AI likeness generation without consent.

NIST AI RMF supplies the shared vocabulary (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage; 7 trustworthiness characteristics) and the GenAI Profile (AI 600-1) adds 12 GenAI risks — 'confabulation' and 'value chain and component integration' are the two most procurement-relevant, framing demands for model cards, training-data provenance, and third-party component disclosure.

State acceptable-use policies converge on triage-relevant rules: NY forbids automated final decisions and requires annual per-system AI risk assessments plus a public AI inventory; NJ requires CTO clearance and registration for resident-facing/decisional GenAI plus prominent disclosure; TX (TRAIGA, eff. Jan 1, 2026) mandates plain-language AI-interaction disclosure and bans social scoring; CT (PA 23-16) requires pre-implementation impact assessments and a public vendor-naming AI inventory.

Checkable registries for the wizard's 'can we verify basic legitimacy' step: GovAI AI Registry on Hortus Trellis (has the vendor filed a FactSheet?), Pavilion AI Contract Hub (does any agency have a live contract?), CT and NY public AI inventories (already deployed in a state?), SAM.gov, and StateRAMP/TX-RAMP/FedRAMP marketplaces (security authorization).

NASPO's flagship publication (the Oct 2024 NASPO/NASCIO 'AI-Powered Procurement' report) is about using AI inside procurement operations, not evaluating AI vendors — NASPO offers no vendor-question checklist comparable to GovAI's, so the wizard should lean on GovAI, OMB, and California instead.

The deduplicated master list lands at ~34 recurring questions across seven themes (data, security, accuracy, transparency, lock-in, pricing, support); the highest-signal openers for a triage tool are: 'Will our data train your models?', 'Which underlying models exactly?', 'Show measured accuracy for OUR use case and let us test with data you can't see', 'Which agencies use this today?', and 'Will you certify NIST AI RMF-consistent governance?'

Currency traps to encode: STD 1000 is retired (don't tell users to request it); M-24-18 is rescinded; WaTech's interim guidelines page is gone (cite DATA-04); NY's policy was re-issued June 24, 2026 under a new Chief AI Office; Colorado SB 24-205's status needs re-verification before citing (implementation was delayed to mid-2026).

Several key .gov sources actively block scripted fetching (sanjoseca.gov 403s, expired certs at calpia/cga.ct.gov) — the wizard's research pipeline needs cached copies or reader-proxy fallbacks for exactly the most important primary documents.

Classify every compliance claim into one of four buckets: attestation (SOC 2, PCI AOC — no registry, request the document), registry-backed authorization (FedRAMP, GovRAMP, TX-RAMP, ISO 27001, Visa/Mastercard PCI lists, CSA STAR — auto-checkable), contract-based regime (HIPAA BAA, FERPA DPA, CJIS Addendum, IRS Pub 1075 Exhibit 7 — no certification exists), and framework alignment (NIST 800-53/171 — unverifiable self-claim unless backed by an assessment).

StateRAMP rebranded to GovRAMP on Feb 14, 2025 (legal name reportedly still StateRAMP); its unified Program Participants List at govramp.org/program-participants is public, searchable, updated daily, and Excel-exportable — statuses are Snapshot (progressing), Core (60 controls, PMO-reviewed), Ready (~80 controls, 3PAO), Provisionally Authorized, and Authorized (full NIST 800-53 Rev 5 baseline, ~319 controls at Moderate).

FedRAMP is the best automated-verification target in the landscape: the authoritative marketplace at fedramp.gov/marketplace is backed by daily-updated public JSON at github.com/FedRAMP/marketplace-fedramp-gov-data (data.json, fedramp-status-changelog.json, products file), with schemas at github.com/FedRAMP/schemas — the tool can diff vendor claims against it directly, including status history.

SOC 2 has NO public registry and is an attestation, not a certification — verification means requesting the full report under NDA, checking the CPA firm via CPAverify (ald.nasba.org/search/cpa) and the AICPA Peer Review Public File Search, confirming an unqualified opinion, a period ending within 12 months (bridge letter for gaps), and a scope covering the actual product; Type I = controls designed at a point in time, Type II = controls operated effectively over 3-12 months.

There is no such thing as 'CJIS certified' — the FBI CJIS ISO Program states in writing that no CJIS certification process exists; compliance is state-by-state via the CJIS Security Addendum, fingerprint background checks, and CSA audits (some states like Colorado CBI and Georgia GBI publish vendor lists); current policy is v6.1 (June 2026) after the major v6.0 modernization.

HHS explicitly says no HIPAA certification exists and it endorses no private seal; the real mechanism is the signed BAA — 'HIPAA compliant' with no willingness to sign a BAA is the definitive red flag, and a BAA plus current SOC 2 Type II (or HITRUST) is materially stronger than a BAA alone.

FedRAMP overstatement vocabulary to auto-flag: 'FedRAMP compliant', 'equivalent', 'attested', 'built on a FedRAMP Authorized platform' — none are recognized terms; 'FedRAMP Ready' is real but covers only ~30-40 of 325 Moderate controls; only 'Authorized' on the marketplace carries OMB's presumption of adequacy. Absence of FedRAMP is normal for SLED-only vendors and should not be penalized.

TX-RAMP (mandatory for Texas state agency cloud contracts) publishes its certified products list at dir.texas.gov as periodic Excel exports with acknowledged publishing gaps (fallback: txramp@dir.texas.gov); Provisional status allows contracting for 18 months but is not certification, and since Oct 30, 2024 FedRAMP/StateRAMP status no longer auto-converts — vendors must file a reciprocity request.

ISO 27001 is verifiable via the free public IAF CertSearch (iafcertsearch.org, with bulk/API options) plus the certification body's own register — but check accreditation (certificate mills exist), expiry, the 2022-edition transition, and especially the scope statement, since a cert scoped to corporate HQ says nothing about the SaaS product.

'NIST compliant' is an unverifiable self-claim: 800-53 is the catalog underlying FedRAMP/GovRAMP/TX-RAMP (the verifiable versions of the claim), and 800-171 self-attested SPRS scores are DoD-visible only and demonstrably unreliable — MORSECORP paid $4.6M under the False Claims Act in March 2025 after self-reporting 104 while ~78% of controls were missing.

PCI DSS has two public opt-in registries — Visa's Global Registry of Service Providers (visa.com/splisting/searchGrsp.do) and Mastercard's SDP Compliant list (PDF) — where presence means QSA-validated compliance with annual revalidation, but absence does not mean non-compliance; the universal check is the current AOC signed by a named QSA.

IRS Pub 1075 and FERPA have no vendor certification or public registry: FTI access requires the AGENCY to file a 45-day IRS notification and put Exhibit 7 language in the contract; FERPA compliance is created by DPAs (the SDPC National DPA v2 is the de facto standard, but the SDPC registry went members-only in Jan 2022).

Fair small-vendor bar: a 10-person startup should have SOC 2 Type I (or Type II underway with a named auditor — automation platforms put this in the low tens of thousands of dollars), a pen test letter, trust center, subprocessor list, DPA, and willingness to sign the applicable BAA/NDPA/CJIS Addendum; GovRAMP's Security Snapshot costs $1,000 for sub-$1M-revenue firms, so 'are you at least in the Snapshot program' is a fair ask — demanding FedRAMP/GovRAMP Authorized, HITRUST, or ISO+SOC 2 together is not.

Five artifacts any legitimate vendor of any size can produce within days: a third-party pen test summary (within 12 months, named firm), a security whitepaper/trust center, a subprocessor list (for AI vendors: which model providers receive agency data and under what terms), a DPA with concrete breach-notification timelines, and an incident response plan summary with a named contact — inability to produce ANY of these means no security program exists.

Size-independent auto-flags for the wizard: claiming certifications that don't exist ('CJIS/HIPAA/FERPA/NIST certified'), claims contradicted by the FedRAMP JSON, GovRAMP list, TX-RAMP XLSX, IAF CertSearch, or Visa registry, a hyperscaler's compliance passed off as the vendor's own ('we're SOC 2/FedRAMP because we run on AWS'), refusal to share any report even under NDA, and 'in progress' claims with no auditor name, engagement letter, or snapshot on file.

USAspending.gov is the best single check: free, no API key, no auth, JSON (api.usaspending.gov) — POST /api/v2/autocomplete/recipient/ resolves a name to UEIs and /api/v2/search/spending_by_award/ proves actual federal payments; federal-only is its one blind spot.

WHOIS/RDAP domain age is the cheapest fraud tripwire: free, keyless JSON via rdap.org bootstrap (or IANA's dns.json) returns registration date and registrar in one call — a months-old domain contradicting 'years serving government' claims is a decisive red flag.

SAM.gov Entity Management API (api.sam.gov/entity-information, free public key from a SAM account) proves TIN-validated legal existence with UEI, addresses, and registration dates; pair every call with the Exclusions API debarment check — but daily quotas vary by account role (reported 10 to 1,000/day) and must be verified empirically before building.

FPDS is dying: ezSearch was decommissioned Feb 24, 2026 and the ATOM feed follows later in FY 2026 — build on USAspending or the new SAM.gov Contract Awards API (searchable by awardeeLegalBusinessName/UEI), never on FPDS.

Cooperative purchasing contract-holder lists are public and loginless at Sourcewell (with a downloadable full-contract XLSX — nearly API-grade), NASPO ValuePoint, OMNIA Partners, and PEPPM; a listing proves a competitively awarded contract. TIPS is public in-browser but returned 403 to automated fetching.

City/state checkbook portals are the gold standard for proving real SLED customers: Checkbook NYC has a free keyless XML API (contracts + spending, 20K records/call), and Socrata-based state portals (NY, CT, and others) expose free SODA JSON endpoints; coverage is a patchwork requiring a hand-built registry of endpoints.

There is no free 50-state Secretary of State API: OpenCorporates covers all 50 states + DC but charges roughly £2,250+/yr for API access — however it grants free public-benefit API access on application, and a free open-source New America-affiliated tool is a plausible fit; free per-state fallbacks exist (data.ny.gov SODA dataset n9v6-gdp6, data.colorado.gov, Florida Sunbiz bulk FTP).

GSA eLibrary (gsaelibrary.gsa.gov) is searchable without login and presence there means GSA-vetted schedule holder — a very strong green flag with no API but stable scrapable pages; absence is neutral since most SLED AI startups hold no schedule.

crt.sh certificate transparency (?q=domain&output=json, free, no key) corroborates how long real infrastructure has existed and whether product subdomains (app., api.) back up the marketing site — but the endpoint is undocumented and overload-prone, so cache and degrade gracefully.

Do not automate LinkedIn: no public company API, ToS prohibit scraping, and LinkedIn's 2025 suit shut down Proxycurl entirely — generate a pre-built search link and tell users what to verify manually (employee count vs. claims).

Crunchbase killed its free API tier (~2025; entry access now ~$588–$1,188+/yr) and GovSpend/SmartProcure is demo-gated at a reported ~$11.6K/yr median — neither fits a free tool; BBB has no official API and near-zero B2G relevance; BidNet/DemandStar sit behind registration walls.

CourtListener/RECAP (free API key) searches hundreds of millions of federal docket entries by party name for litigation context, but 2026 default rate limits are tight (~125 requests/day) — cache results or get a Free Law Project membership for expanded access.

GDELT DOC 2.0 gives free JSON news search with boolean operators but only a rolling ~3-month window — use it as a recent-coverage check, discount wire-service press releases to zero, and supplement with a generated Google News RSS link.

The checks compose into a cost-ordered funnel: RDAP + crt.sh (instant, universal) → SAM + USAspending (federal identity and revenue) → state incorporation → cooperative lists + checkbook portals (SLED customers); single misses are neutral — the red-flag pattern is contradiction across sources, the green-flag pattern is convergence.
GitHub org lookup (api.github.com/orgs/<org>, 60/hr unauthenticated or 5,000/hr with a free token) is a cheap corroboration check specifically apt for AI vendors claiming engineering depth.

Regulatory anchors exist for nearly every red flag: FTC Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024, ongoing through 2026) and SEC AI-washing cases give the tool enforcement-grade precedent — DoNotPay ('robot lawyer'), Workado (claimed 98% accuracy, actual 53%), accessiBe ($1M, 'AI makes any site WCAG-compliant'), IntelliVision ('zero bias'), Presto (third-party AI sold as proprietary), Joonko (forged customer contracts and testimonials), Nate ($40M 'AI' that was a Philippine call center).

The best government-specific cautionary tales are Evolv (FTC: 'AI weapons detection' oversold to 800+ schools; settlement bans accuracy, speed, and labor-cost claims and let K-12 customers cancel), Banjo (Utah auditor: ~$21M contract to a vendor whose claimed AI likely didn't exist, awarded without verification), Deloitte Australia (partial refund after AI-hallucinated citations in a government report), and ShotSpotter (marketing-department-derived '97% accuracy' that audits could not reproduce).

Air AI — sued by the FTC in Aug 2025 over claims its AI could replace human customer-service reps — is directly on point, since AI call-center operations is the #1 use case pitched to state benefits agencies per the New America survey.

Domain forensics is fully automatable and free: RDAP (rdap.org/domain/{domain}) for registration date vs. claimed company age, Wayback CDX API for earliest crawl and what the domain used to host, and crt.sh (?output=json) for first-certificate date plus subdomain census (a real SaaS has app/api/docs/status subdomains; a facade has only www).

The single highest-value check is verifying claimed government customers, and it is uniquely feasible because public procurement leaves public records: agency site: searches, Legistar/Granicus council agendas, USAspending/SAM.gov by UEI, state checkbook portals, cooperative-contract directories (NASPO ValuePoint, Sourcewell, OMNIA), and ultimately a call to the agency's procurement office or a records request. A case study that exists nowhere but the vendor's own site is a high-severity flag; agency denial is critical.

Compliance vocabulary is diagnostic and registry-checkable: 'FedRAMP compliant/ready/equivalent' is explicitly not FedRAMP Authorized per fedramp.gov (check marketplace.fedramp.gov); state/local analog is GovRAMP (ex-StateRAMP) Authorized Product List; 'HIPAA certified' and 'CJIS certified' are nonexistent certifications (HHS/OCR certifies nothing; CJIS is per-agreement); SOC 2 is an attestation report you must ask to see, not a badge.

AI-text detection must never be a primary signal: OpenAI retired its own classifier (26% recall, 9% false positives), Stanford found >61% of non-native-speaker writing misclassified, and no tool in a 14-detector test hit 80% accuracy. AI-tell words ('delve' up 654% in abstracts) are corroborating context only — by 2026 legitimate vendors draft with AI too. Specificity (falsifiable facts vs. unfalsifiable superlatives) discriminates better than style.

AI-generated team photos are detectable: LinkedIn's published method catches 99.6% of StyleGAN faces at 1% false positives; practical tells are over-symmetric eyes, warped backgrounds, mangled ears and hair; reverse-image search (TinEye API) catches stock-photo 'leadership teams.' Diffusion-generated faces are harder — treat detector output as probabilistic.

Virtual-office/registered-agent addresses presented as operating HQ are a recognized shell-company signal from AML practice (banks demand leases/utility bills for exactly this reason) — automatable by geocoding the address, classifying the place type, and counting cohabiting companies; but registered-agent use for legal mail alone is universal and innocent.

The 'thin GPT wrapper' flag is about misrepresentation, not architecture: the Presto SEC case (third-party speech tech described as proprietary, 'eliminates humans' while humans did most orders) and Builder.ai (700 human developers behind an 'AI' platform, revenue inflated ~300%) define the two failure modes — fake AI provenance and hidden human labor. Ask which foundation model, whose API key, where PII flows, and what the model provider's terms permit.

Classic govtech red-flag claims now have enforcement precedent: guaranteed savings/earnings percentages (Ascend Ecom, Click Profit, FBA Machine), unqualified accuracy claims ('100%', 'detects all', 'zero bias' — Evolv, Workado, IntelliVision), premature availability claims, deceptive demos, and perception-based productivity stats (all named as current FTC enforcement patterns in Holland & Knight's Aug 2026 two-year retrospective).

Severity calibration rule: only registry contradictions (fake FedRAMP/GovRAMP claim, nonexistent legal entity, SAM.gov debarment, agency-denied customer claim, fabricated people) should alone produce 'do not engage'; probabilistic detectors (AI text/image) and single soft signals (young domain, template site) only corroborate. The tool should also surface green flags (verified customers, real attestations, completed GovAI FactSheet).

The GovAI Coalition's AI FactSheet (NIST AI RMF-aligned, vendor-completed, 150+ member agencies, San José-led) is a ready-made standardized 'next step' the wizard can output: asking a vendor to complete it costs the officer nothing, and refusal is itself a signal. Vendor-agreement and incident-response templates exist in the same free library.

Practical build notes: FTC.gov and sanjoseca.gov blocked automated fetching (403) — the tool's own research layer needs fallbacks for .gov sources; LinkedIn footprint checks must be guided-manual (no public API, scraping violates ToS); LinkedIn company-page creation-date visibility is unverified — confirm in-product before promising that check; the Rytr consent-order reversal (Dec 2025) rests on a single secondary source and needs verification; all API endpoint shapes cited were verified against documentation, not live calls.

Every marquee AI-vendor fraud of 2024-26 (Nate, Joonko, Presto, Builder.ai, Frank/Javice) was detectable via public founder/team signals, and SEC/DOJ/FTC now treat 'AI-washing' as a named enforcement priority — founder diligence is the highest-yield triage check (sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-70; sec.gov/enforcement-litigation/litigation-releases/lr-26282).

Best free/cheap programmatic checks: SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q=..., no key, User-Agent header required), SEC SALI individual-action lookup, CourtListener RECAP v4 API for federal dockets/parties, OpenCorporates officer search (140+ jurisdictions), SAM.gov Exclusions API (open.gsa.gov/api/exclusions-api/), OpenSanctions matching API, PatentsView inventor API, OpenAlex + Semantic Scholar + ORCID for publications, GitHub REST API for real engineering activity, Wayback CDX API for bio-drift/title-inflation detection, RDAP for domain age, GDELT DOC 2.0 for news corroboration.

The tool must NOT scrape LinkedIn: hiQ ended with a $500K judgment, established breach-of-contract liability, and a permanent injunction (Dec 2022), and LinkedIn's 2025 suit shut down Proxycurl with an injunction reaching its customers — instead emit 'manual check cards' deep-linking the user to the company People tab and founder profiles with a 60-second checklist (employee count vs claims, engineering titles, profile ages).

Adopt tri-state findings — VERIFIED / COULD NOT VERIFY / OFFICIAL RECORD FOUND — and never convert absence of evidence into accusation: 'we could not verify this claim from public sources' is defensible; 'fake bio,' 'shell company,' or 'fraudster' about a named person is libel-per-se territory (crime/professional-unfitness imputations carry presumed damages).

Negative information about named people should ride almost exclusively on the fair report privilege: fair, substantially accurate, attributed, dated summaries of official records (SEC releases, court dockets, debarment lists) with links, 'alleged' for unadjudicated matters, and outcomes noted — recognized in every state but Maine (firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/fair-report-privilege/).

Assume Section 230 does not protect the tool's own generated output and that disclaimers alone are inadequate (Volokh, 'Large Libel Models,' 3 J. Free Speech L. 489); Walters v. OpenAI (Ga. May 2025) shows caveats and user sophistication can defeat claims, but it involved a public figure with no damages — a private-figure founder who loses a government deal is the opposite fact pattern, and most founders are private figures subject only to a negligence standard.

Wrong-person matching is the #1 operational risk (Bing fused two different Battles into one defamatory bio; FTC's $5.8M TruthFinder/Instant Checkmate order punished loose matching): require at least two corroborating identifiers before attaching any record to a person, apply the strictest threshold to negative official records, auto-downgrade confidence on common names, and hedge with 'records matching this name.'

Stay out of FCRA scope: restrict person-level checks to individuals the vendor holds out as leadership, frame everything as vendor-entity evaluation for a commercial transaction, and prominently bar use for employment/credit/tenant/insurance decisions — marketing and foreseeable use, not disclaimers, determined CRA status in the FTC's TruthFinder case.

Team-composition signal: a genuine AI company shows engineers in public (LinkedIn titles, job postings, engineering blog, GitHub org with members and substantive repos, patents, papers); zero technical footprint is a soft flag to convert into a demo question — and contractor-heavy delivery is only fraud when misrepresented as AI (Builder.ai's ~700 humans behind 'Natasha').

Stock-photo/AI-generated team pages are a real documented scam pattern, but automated GAN detection is unreliable — output the observation (reverse-image-search hit counts via Google Lens/TinEye manual cards, no professional footprint for any listed person) and route to human review rather than asserting 'fake employees.'

Title inflation and bio drift are cheaply detectable with the Wayback CDX API (web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=vendor.com/about&output=json&collapse=digest): diff archived team pages over time and present both dated artifacts without asserting motive.

Serial shell-company detection via OpenCorporates officer search plus registered-agent/address clustering works but has the worst name-collision and data-gap profile (Delaware exposes little officer data) — describe registry results neutrally with counts and links, never as a 'shell company' accusation.

Publish a research-methods page listing every source consulted and show all evidence inline: opinions based on fully disclosed true facts are constitutionally protected, so 'showing the work' is simultaneously the defamation defense, the GDPR/CCPA transparency story, and the trust feature for skeptical government users.

Build a notice-and-correction channel ('Are you this vendor? Report an error') with fast human review and takedown-on-notice — once on notice of a specific false statement, continued publication can satisfy even the actual-malice standard; also timestamp every report and let findings expire rather than caching stale negatives.

Positive verification can rest on light evidence, negative implication requires official records, and the tool's strongest legitimate 'bad vendor' output evaluates the pitch, not the person: 'basic legitimacy could not be verified from public sources — do not engage until the vendor provides incorporation details, named government references, and technical staff bios.'

The market has three layers requiring different diligence: CCaaS/hyperscaler platforms (AWS Connect, Google Customer Engagement Suite ex-CCAI, Genesys, NICE, Five9, Talkdesk), the integrators who actually deliver them to states (Deloitte TrueServe, Accenture, Smartronix, Quantiphi, C1 Gov, Maximus), and startups (govtech-native Polimorphic/Citibot vs. commercial Sierra/Decagon/PolyAI, the latter with no verified U.S. state/local deployments publicly listed).

Named, sourced government reference deployments exist and should be the wizard's benchmark set: Illinois IDES (Google CCAI on Cisco, 140K inquiries/day), Texas TWC 'Larry' (Accenture+AWS, 21M questions), Colorado CDLE (phased Google virtual agent), Workforce West Virginia (Amazon Connect in 72 hours), South Carolina DSS (19 centers), Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (900K chatbot interactions/month), Minnesota DVS (4-language chatbot), NJ 211 (Five9), Kyle TX (Agentforce), Amarillo 'Emma', plus IRS voice bots and USCIS Emma as federal analogs.

Realistic containment anchors: Tamarac FL's vendor-published 20% full self-service is the honest municipal number; high rates (WV's 90%) occurred only on narrow scripted FAQ surge lines; Gartner's own bullish forecast is 80% of *common* issues by *2029* — so any pitch claiming 80-90%+ containment today should trigger the formula-and-reference demand.

Containment is gameable: abandoned calls, IVR completions, and 'caller didn't reply' are routinely counted as contained; the wizard should teach the metric 'fully resolved without human AND without abandonment' and demand transcript audit rights (Platform28: ~98% of government calls go unreviewed).

Hallucinated benefit guidance on official channels is the category's signature failure: NYC MyCity told businesses to break the law (The Markup, Mar 2024), and the Air Canada tribunal ruling (Feb 2024) established the deployer owns everything its bot says — good systems are retrieval-grounded on approved content, cite sources, refuse-and-escalate, and never render eligibility determinations.

Human escalation must be unconditional: IRS voice bots always allow a representative; Klarna's public reversal of its 'AI replaced 700 agents' strategy (Forbes, May 2025) is the standing rebuttal to FTE-replacement pitches; a no-exit bot is a due-process problem for benefits populations.

Language access is where deployments visibly fail: a Washington state agency removed an AI voice in Feb 2026 after Spanish-line callers got Spanish-accented English (StateScoop); '75+ languages supported' means machine translation, not access — Minnesota DVS's community-informed 4-language build is the benchmark; EO 14224 (Mar 2025) revoked the federal LEP mandate but Title VI persists, so treat vendor claims either way as unsettled.

Pricing has four models with verified ranges: per-seat ($72-$240/user/mo across NICE, Genesys, Five9, Talkdesk; Five9 has a 50-seat minimum), consumption (Amazon Connect $0.038/voice-min, $0.010/chat message), per-resolution ($0.99 Intercom Fin; Salesforce and HubSpot both switched to per-resolution in 2026), and startup flat subscriptions — government quotes then add integration, telephony passthrough, and AI metering on top.

Per-resolution pricing is currently unstable and gameable: Intercom bills an 'outcome' when the customer merely stops replying; TechTarget (Aug 2026) calls resolution measurement an unsolved problem; Gartner (Jan 2026) predicts GenAI cost-per-resolution will exceed offshore human agent costs by 2030 — states should not sign multi-year per-resolution deals without contractual resolution definitions and audit rights.

Voice AI carries specific legal exposure: FCC 24-17 (Feb 2024) makes AI-generated/cloned voices 'artificial voices' under the TCPA requiring prior express consent for outbound calls; California SB 1001 and Utah's AI Policy Act require bot disclosure; the Colorado AI Act (high-risk category includes government services) took effect June 30, 2026; FBI warnings (2025) about cloned official voices make 'indistinguishable from human' a liability, not a feature.

Fast verification registries the wizard can check programmatically: FedRAMP Marketplace (product-level, not company-level — Genesys and Talkdesk hold authorizations), GovRAMP (renamed from StateRAMP Feb 14, 2025; Authorized Product List, 330+ products), TX-RAMP, SAM.gov, and Carahsoft/NASPO resale listings; 'FedRAMP compliant' without a marketplace listing is a red flag.

The lowest-risk entry point is agent-assist/after-call-work (summarization, real-time knowledge retrieval — e.g., Verizon's 28,000-rep Gemini assistant), which has no resident-facing hallucination surface; the wizard can steer overwhelmed agencies toward asking vendors for this before any resident-facing bot.

The public accountability metrics already exist: CMS forced states to publish call center average wait time and abandonment rate during Medicaid unwinding (Georgetown CCF, CBPP tracking) — AI proposals should commit to moving those published numbers, not proprietary deflection metrics.

Deployment speed claims need context: the famous fast launches (TWC Larry in 5 days, West Virginia in 72 hours) were scripted FAQ bots during the 2020 surge; anything integrated with claim status or eligibility systems takes months — 'days to deploy' plus 'fully integrated' in one pitch is self-contradicting.

Platform modernization does not fix program problems: California's billion-dollar EDDNext still faced fraud and debt criticism (KQED, Dec 2024), and Illinois's widely-cited '$100M annual savings' was an initial vendor-published estimate — the wizard should default-label all vendor case-study metrics as vendor-reported.

Document processing is the #2 pitched AI use case for benefits agencies (per the April-May 2026 New America survey in the project brief); the vendor field is 100+ companies, with Gartner's first-ever IDP Magic Quadrant (Sept 2025) naming five Leaders: ABBYY, Hyperscience, Infrrd, Tungsten Automation, UiPath (gartner.com/en/documents/6912666).

Strong named government anchors exist for the wizard: SSA + Hyperscience/Accenture ($81M, 250M docs/yr), VA mail sorting 10 days to half a day (confirmed by GAO-26-109137), Colorado HCPF and Missouri DSS SNAP/MAGI (Hyperscience), California DMV + ABBYY (65-70% automation), Covered California + Google Document AI (84% verification), King County WA + Textract redaction (96%, human-reviewed), Hawaii + Document AI, Arkansas Judiciary + CSI Intellidact, Pierce County WA + Extract Systems.

The central failure mode is the clean-demo-to-production gap: buyers consistently report 15-25 percentage point accuracy drops on their own document mix, and '99% character accuracy' can mean ~80% field accuracy; at 97% field accuracy a 20-field form is error-free only ~55% of the time (airparser.com/blog/ai-document-extraction-accuracy-benchmarks/).

Realistic production numbers from actual government deployments are 65-84% automation/verification - so any pitch promising 95%+ straight-through processing or 'no human review' before piloting on the agency's own faxes, phone photos, and handwriting should trigger skepticism.

Independent oversight documents real failures: VA OIG 22-02936-175 found 27% of automation-assisted hypertension claims had inaccurate determinations; TIGTA (Feb 2026) found IRS missed its paperless processing goals and raised non-competitive award concerns; GAO-26-109137 (July 2026) flags AI opacity as an accountability risk.

Per-page pricing surprises are quantifiable: plain OCR is ~$1.50/1,000 pages at all three hyperscalers, but full extraction is $30-70/1,000 (20-47x), features stack per page (Textract Forms+Tables+Queries = $0.070/page), and human review adds $30/1,000 reviewed pages (Amazon A2I) plus roughly 3+ FTEs per 200,000 exception pages/year.

PII defaults differ sharply: AWS may use Textract inputs to improve its AI services unless the agency sets an AWS Organizations opt-out policy; Azure deletes inputs within 24 hours and never trains on them; Google Document AI never trains on customer content and is FedRAMP High - the wizard should ask every vendor for written retention/no-training terms.

Verification anchors a non-technical officer can check in minutes: FedRAMP Marketplace, the GovRAMP (ex-StateRAMP) Authorized Product List (Tungsten TotalAgility Cloud is GovRAMP Authorized; Hyperscience claims FedRAMP High/IL5), SAM.gov CAGE/UEI, and named press-covered references.

Even market leaders use aggressive tactics: Hyperscience's April 2026 SNAP 4-pager (hosted by APHSA) claims '99.5% accuracy and 98% automation,' calls itself 'the only solution on the market,' and explicitly coaches states on sole-source procurement justification - skepticism triggers must apply to incumbents, not just startups.

Redaction is its own sub-market with asymmetric risk (a missed SSN = a disclosure): county/court specialists Extract Systems ID Shield and CSI Intellidact have long-running deployments; demand precision AND recall reported separately plus a QA process for misses.

What good looks like: field-level accuracy on the agency's own documents, calibrated confidence scores routing to a staffed human review queue, named format/language coverage, per-document audit trails (model version, confidence, human touches) exportable for IG review, and drift monitoring - all demonstrated in a 250-1,000-document pilot including the ugly documents.

Many cold pitches are thin wrappers over Textract/Azure/Google APIs or a commercial LLM; asking 'what engine is under the hood and which subprocessors touch our documents' is a high-yield triage question that also surfaces unvetted data flows.

Anchor numbers for the wizard's cost sanity-check: SSA's comparable is $81M for 250M docs/yr at federal scale; a 1M-page/yr state document flow costs roughly $70k/yr in hyperscaler API fees at full-feature rates before license, integration, and review labor.

Treat this as the constitutional category: Goldberg v. Kelly and 42 CFR 431.210 / 7 CFR 273.13 mean every AI-influenced adverse action needs specific, regulation-citing, appeal-ready reasons — generic AI explanations are per se inadequate (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/397/254).

OMB M-25-21 (Apr 2025, current policy) presumes AI in benefits adjudication, continued-eligibility determination, fraud detection, and benefits penalties is 'high-impact,' mandating pre-deployment testing, impact assessments, human oversight with fail-safes, appeals, and discontinuation if non-compliant — the natural diligence benchmark for states (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf).

The cautionary canon is deep and named: Michigan MiDAS (>90% wrong auto-fraud findings, $20M settlement, vendor suits vs. SAS/FAST), Australia Robodebt (A$1.76B unlawful debts, Royal Commission), Arkansas ARChoices and Idaho K.W. v. Armstrong (algorithms invalidated; 'trade secret' defense rejected), Tennessee TEDS/A.M.C. v. Smith (2024: Medicaid Act + due process + ADA violations).

Even deterministic incumbent systems fail at scale: KFF found Deloitte eligibility systems in 25 states ($5B+ contracts) generated wrong notices, wrong addresses, and mass erroneous terminations; July 2026 NPR/KFF reporting shows Michigan disability miscategorization continuing — so 'established vendor' is not a safety proxy in this category (https://kffhealthnews.org/news/article/medicaid-deloitte-run-eligibility-systems-plagued-by-errors/).

2026-specific risk wave: OBBBA work-requirement implementation is forcing rushed eligibility-system changes (est. 7.5M Medicaid / 2.4M SNAP losses by 2034), spawning 'AI for verification/exemption screening' pitches that are adverse-action engines and belong in the highest caution band (https://www.tpr.org/news/2026-07-21/deloitte-run-systems-denied-medicaid-to-disabled-people-new-laws-could-make-it-worse).

The bright line for triage: AI that assembles/summarizes/drafts with a named human deciding every adverse action is evaluable; AI that decides (auto-denial, auto-termination, auto-fraud-flag) should never score low-risk — matching NY's LOADinG Act meaningful-human-review statute and Nava PBC's published guardrails.

Landscape splits into five lanes with different risk: integrators/COTS (Deloitte, Accenture, Gainwell, Conduent, Maximus, Merative Curam, Salesforce/ServiceNow), document AI (Hyperscience — FedRAMP High, named SSA/CO/MO deployments, confidence-threshold human review), caseworker copilots (Nava toolkit, Augintel, Northwoods), applicant navigators (Maryland+Anthropic, mRelief, MyFriendBen), and fraud/identity vendors — the last lane always adverse-action.

LLM-specific failure modes to encode: confident hallucination of stale rules (NYC MyCity told users to break the law for 2 years before its Jan 2026 shutdown), nondeterministic answers as an equal-treatment defect, post-hoc rationalization that can't populate legal notices, automation bias/rubber-stamping, upstream document-extraction errors, multilingual/disability gaps, and prompt injection/PII leakage (https://themarkup.org/artificial-intelligence/2024/03/29/nycs-ai-chatbot-tells-businesses-to-break-the-law).

Killer diligence questions: show the actual denial notice; commit contractually to full record disclosure at fair hearings (no trade-secret objections); state-specific accuracy with denominators and demographic breakouts; caseworker override rates (near-zero = rubber stamp); rollback/mass-reinstatement plan; APD/CMS/FNS approval awareness (45 CFR 95.611).

Skepticism triggers: 'fully automated eligibility,' fraud-reduction percentages without false-positive rates, '99% accuracy' without denominators, 'unbiased AI,' 'proprietary — can't share,' 'deploy in weeks,' 'FedRAMP compliant' (vs. authorized — verify in marketplace), 'human in the loop' without numbers, free pilots contingent on broad data access.

State law is moving but unsettled: Texas TRAIGA effective Jan 1, 2026 (govt AI disclosure); Colorado AI Act delayed to June 30, 2026 with 2026 status uncertain — the wizard should date-stamp and re-verify statutory claims rather than hard-code them.

Reference infrastructure exists for the tool to cite: Benefits Tech Advocacy Hub case studies (btah.org, run by NHeLP/Upturn/TechTonic Justice), TechTonic Justice's Inescapable AI (92M low-income Americans affected), CDT's litigation guide, Beeck Center Digital Benefits Network AI resources, and Code for America's 2026 Government AI Landscape Assessment naming MD/NJ/NC/PA/TX/UT/VT as leading states.

Positive deployment pattern to reward in scoring: asymmetric automation (auto-approve/renew with audit sampling; never auto-deny), retrieval grounded in the state's current policy manual with citations and refusal behavior, immutable audit trails including model/corpus versions, GovRAMP/FedRAMP + SOC 2 Type II, no vendor training on agency data, and published evaluations.

Liability reaches vendors, not just agencies (Cahoo v. SAS posture; Deloitte's 'they're not our systems' defense) — indemnification, audit rights, and error-correction SLAs are contract-level diligence items the wizard should prompt users to demand.

Caveat for the build: the April–May 2026 New America survey is not publicly indexed (treat as internal context); the CMS 2023 ex parte reinstatement figures (~500k, ~30 states) and some fraud-vendor specifics could not be re-verified this session and should be confirmed before the tool quotes them.

NYC MyCity is the canonical public-comms cautionary tale with a complete arc: launched Oct 2023 on Microsoft's cloud, caught telling businesses to break the law (The Markup, Mar 2024), kept alive behind a 'beta' disclaimer, and finally shut down Feb 4, 2026 after ~$600K build + ~$500K/yr maintenance — disclaimer-instead-of-fix and sunk-cost inertia are the failure patterns to screen for.

Moffatt v. Air Canada (Feb 2024) established that an organization is liable for its chatbot's statements — the 'chatbot is a separate entity' defense failed — so chatbot diligence must include indemnification terms and legal sign-off on high-stakes answer domains.

The resident-chatbot market is fragmented and cheap to enter: Polimorphic, Citibot, Tyler, Verint, Zammo, NeuroSoph, Capgemini and others, with contracts from ~$5,600 to $759,000+; named deployments with claimed metrics exist (Georgia 'George A.I.' 2.5M users/97% claimed accuracy; Massachusetts 'Ask MA' ~1.2M monthly users) but accuracy figures are self-reported.

Machine translation is a policy flashpoint in 2025-26: DOJ's July 2025 memo pushes agencies toward AI translation under the English-official-language EO, while NCSC/digital.gov guidance requires human review for consequential documents and documents that MT degrades badly on low-resource languages; New Jersey DOL's plain-language-first Spanish UI translation assistant (April 2024, with USDR) is the replicable good example.

For staff productivity, Microsoft 365 Copilot (GCC Dec 2024, GCC High Dec 2025, free 12 months via GSA OneGov with G5) and Google Gemini for Government ($0.47/agency federal OneGov deal) are commoditized incumbents — the wizard's first productivity-pack question should be 'what does this startup do that the copilot you already own doesn't?'

Pennsylvania's ChatGPT Enterprise pilot is the best-documented state deployment: 175 employees/14 agencies, self-reported ~95 min/day saved, 85% positive, now expanded past 3,000 employees — but its ROI numbers are participant-reported, a skepticism the wizard should model for all vendor ROI claims.

AI-generated content is a public record: Washington State Archives advises both prompts and outputs are likely records retained by content not format, and MRSC flags that Copilot's activity history apparently can't be disabled — records-export/retention-control contract terms are a make-or-break diligence item.

AI notetakers carry live litigation risk: Brewer v. Otter.ai (Aug 2025, now four consolidated federal cases) tests the recording-without-all-party-consent design pattern; for governments, add closed-session leakage, uncontrolled third-party retention, and FOIA discoverability of every transcript.

Shadow AI is quantified and real: 69% of orgs suspect prohibited GenAI use (Gartner 2025), 78% of AI users BYO tools (Microsoft WTI 2025), and an Oct 2025 NSW incident put 12,000+ rows of flood-victim PII into a public AI tool — a governed sanctioned tool is partly a defense, but only with better data terms.

Data analytics/decision support has the deepest adjudicated harm record in government AI: Michigan MiDAS (93% of reviewed fraud findings wrong, $20M settlement), Idaho K.W. v. Armstrong (trade-secret formula struck down, 2025 contempt), Arkansas RUGs (due-process invalidation), Florida FIRRE (600% flag spike, $92.4M rebuild) — the Benefits Tech Advocacy Hub library (btah.org) catalogs 11 such cases and should be linked from the wizard.

The two analytic failure modes to encode: (1) black-box scores driving adverse actions — courts require contestable explanations and trade-secret shields collapse (K.W., Loomis/COMPAS); (2) base-rate math — IRS fraud filters ran an 81% false-positive rate and delayed $20B in legitimate refunds, so vendor 'accuracy' claims are meaningless without precision at the operating threshold and the flag-queue staffing plan.

A bright triage line for the analytics pack: if a score or flag can by itself trigger an adverse action against a person, it is not a 'dashboard' — route it to a high-risk review track with human-review, notice-text, and disparate-impact questions.

The GovAI Coalition (San José-led) publishes free vendor-facing instruments the wizard can operationalize — the AI FactSheet, model vendor-agreement language, and incident-response templates — so 'ask the vendor to complete a GovAI Coalition AI FactSheet' works as a concrete recommended next step.

Assume Section 230 does NOT protect the tool's own AI-generated evaluations - CRS, CDT, and ABA analyses agree generated output makes the operator an 'information content provider'; 230 still covers user-submitted content the tool merely hosts (congress.gov/crs-product/LSB11097).

Ratings and grades produced by a PUBLISHED, uniform methodology are protected opinion (Castle Rock Remodeling v. BBB, Mo. 2011) - but specific factual sentences inside a report ('not in compliance with licensing requirements,' 'grossly misleading') are actionable even when the grade is not (Budget Van Lines v. BBB, Cal. 2013). The grade is safe; the sentence is the risk.

The single most dangerous failure mode is entity mismatch on legal/enforcement claims: Wolf River Electric v. Google (AI Overview attached other companies' AG lawsuits to the wrong solar firm) is in Minnesota state court with $110-210M claimed damages. Legal-history sections must be retrieval-only with exact-name/UEI match verification, never model memory.

Frame every negative finding as verifiable absence with disclosed search scope: 'We searched SAM.gov, [state] SOS, and USASpending on [date] and found no record matching [name]' - never 'X is fake/a scam/fraudulent.' The asserted fact (we searched and found nothing) is log-provably true; the conclusion stays disclosed-basis opinion under Milkovich.

Ban the vocabulary of intent and crime (scam, fraud, fake, shell, deceptive, misleading, predatory) - these are defamation per se with presumed damages; phrase verdicts as recommendations about the USER's next step ('do not invest staff time until vendor provides X'), not characterizations of the vendor.

Anchor to official records for the fair report privilege: source + date + link + fair-and-accurate portrayal in the same sentence protects the tool even if the underlying government record is wrong (dmlp.org/legal-guide/fair-report-privilege).

Walters v. OpenAI (Ga. 2025) shows disclaimers work only when specific and in-context, plus documented hallucination-mitigation efforts defeated negligence, and the plaintiff's failure to request a retraction mattered; Starbuck v. Meta settled after TWO YEARS of ignored notice - a fast, published correction/dispute process is a damages-limiting legal control, not customer service.

Adopt the U.S. Chamber 'Principles for Fair and Accurate Security Ratings' (2017, signed by BitSight/SecurityScorecard/RiskRecon, FCRA-modeled) as the named governance template: transparency, dispute-correction-appeal with 'disputed' notation until resolved, accuracy/validation, model governance, independence, confidentiality. No defamation suits by rated companies against security raters were found - the self-regulatory framework appears to have pre-empted them.

Publishing the scoring methodology STRENGTHENS the legal posture (opinion doctrine, negligence defense, anti-SLAPP showing) - but misdescribing your own process ('unbiased,' 'verified,' 'comprehensive') creates separate state consumer-protection exposure (Florida BBB FDUTPA case), so market the tool only as what it demonstrably is.

Generate on-demand, date-stamped, expiring reports for the requesting user rather than a browsable public directory of vendor grades; each regeneration is a new publication, so corrections must propagate to all cached copies immediately, and the harshest tier ('could not verify basic legitimacy') should fire only on deterministic, logged registry checks.

Anti-SLAPP: 40 states + DC have statutes (13 UPEPA states as of June 2025) but there is NO federal anti-SLAPP law and several circuits refuse to apply state statutes in federal diversity cases - house the publishing entity in a strong anti-SLAPP jurisdiction (DC works) and carry media-liability/E&O insurance anyway.

License: Apache-2.0 for code (explicit patent grant; Section 6 withholds trademark rights - critical so shoddy forks can't publish 'evaluations' under the tool's name), CC BY 4.0 for methodology docs, trademark the name. Avoid AGPL - many agencies prohibit it and copyleft doesn't protect the actual value (methodology + brand). Note the OSS warranty disclaimer covers the code, not the hosted service's published output; self-hosting agencies become their own publishers.

Terms of use that matter: clickwrap assent, arbitration/venue (binds users only - Battle v. Microsoft was compelled to arbitration because the defamed person was himself a Bing user; a vendor who never used the tool is NOT bound), no-reliance/non-recommendation clause, liability cap, and a published-and-followed correction policy. Theater: buried 'AI may be inaccurate' boilerplate - libel law judges the effect on the average reader, and the defamed vendor is a third party who never saw your TOS.

Keeping the tool free and public-interest-framed is legally load-bearing: government AI spending is a matter of public concern (higher fault standards, anti-SLAPP coverage), whereas ratings distributed privately to select audiences lost First Amendment protection in the credit-rating cases (Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank v. Morgan Stanley) and Dun & Bradstreet v. Greenmoss allowed presumed damages for private-audience credit reports.

Agentic loop gotchas to build for: stop_reason pause_turn requires re-sending assistant content with identical tools; search results re-bill as input each iteration (cache the prefix; dynamic-filtering versions cut this); tool-array changes invalidate prompt caches; batches can slightly exceed workspace spend limits.

One unresolved uncertainty flagged: whether output_config structured outputs can run in the same request as server-side web search is not documented either way — the two-pass design sidesteps it and is cheaper anyway.

planters.com's premium feel decomposes into 5 copyable moves (verified from its live CSS): a tight token palette anchored by one deep blue (#002e5d, 699 uses) plus two pale tints and a cream; solid color-blocked full-width sections instead of white-with-cards; extreme display-type scale contrast (Knockout condensed display vs Degular body); a single pill radius (100px, ~180 declarations); and motion concentrated in one choreographed hero sequence ('Shell-o there!' keyframes) plus marquee text bands — all of which map cleanly onto Source Serif 4 display + cobalt #1F1FD6 + warm neutrals.

Verdict format: use 3-5 named action tiers in plain sentences (NewsGuard model: 'Proceed with Caution' etc.) with fixed color+icon+label, not a 0-100 score or purchase-grade letter — PAIR warns 'novice users may not know whether a value like 80% is low or high,' SSL Labs dropped its numeric display because 'the letter grade is more useful,' and a PLOS One study found label-format comprehension below chance even with simplified numeric labels.

Steal SSL Labs' fatal-flaw mechanics: automatic-override conditions (one disqualifying finding, e.g., unverifiable registration, forces 'do not engage' regardless of other points) and grade caps — never let a weighted average launder a fatal legitimacy flaw.

HIBP is the lay-verdict gold standard: one input, instant plain-spoken verdict ('Good news — no pwnage found!' / 'Oh no — pwned!'), evidence table directly beneath, warm non-jargon tone; Hemingway adds the pattern of highlighting evidence inline on the user's own submitted text — do the same to risky claims inside the pasted pitch.

The honesty panel is the differentiator: a fixed checklist of every check always attempted, each resolving pass / flag / 'could not check (and why)' — modeled on VirusTotal per-engine tri-states, BBB's 'NR' insufficient-information rating, and NewsGuard's alternative designations for unscoreable sites — plus a BBB-style standing disclaimer ('not a guarantee; never a purchase recommendation') and a checked-on timestamp with re-run.

Evidence citation per claim (named source + URL + retrieval date), NewsGuard nutrition-label style, doubles as procurement-file defensibility when printed; layered disclosure (critical factors on the primary layer, detail behind it) is the research-backed label pattern (Emami-Naeini et al.; CHI 2024 found a complexity sweet spot between QR-only and expert-grade labels).

The 1-3 minute wait is a trust asset, not a liability: Buell & Norton's labor illusion (Management Science 2011) shows users value results MORE when shown the work, even preferring longer waits; narrate 4-6 named plain-language stages whose streamed micro-findings ('Found Delaware registration, 2024 ✓') ARE the progress indicator — named exemplars: SSL Labs' live check log, Kayak-style search feeds, Domino's Tracker, USWDS step indicator ('[step] of [total]', aria-current).

NN/g thresholds for the wait design: spinners only for 2-10s, percent-done/step-count indicators beyond ~10s, always a visible way to cancel, and text-paired progress; announce stage changes via aria-live (WCAG 4.1.3 status messages).

Accessibility is now a legal hook for this exact audience: DOJ's ADA Title II rule requires state/local government web content to meet WCAG 2.1 AA by April 26, 2027 (pop ≥50k) / April 26, 2028 (smaller + special districts) — build and advertise the tool as 2.1 AA.

Brand contrast math (computed): cobalt #1F1FD6 passes AA on white (9.44:1) and on warm cream #FAF5E4 (8.65:1), white-on-cobalt passes (9.44:1), charcoal #3B3B3B passes (11.2:1) — but Carolina Blue #21A8E0 on white FAILS for text (2.71:1); never encode tiers by color alone.

Plain language: Plain Writing Act framing plus concrete federal rules (active voice, present tense, shorter words/sections, address the reader as 'you'); target ~8th-grade reading level for verdict copy (average US adult level per Hemingway) and readability-test the tool's own generated output.

Ship a real print/PDF path: @media print stylesheet (even planters.com ships one) — single column, accordions force-expanded, tier labels that survive B&W, full URLs as footnotes, timestamp + 'could not check' always printed; browser print-to-PDF needs no dependencies.

Old-browser strategy: follow USWDS — progressive enhancement ('if JavaScript fails users still get a robust HTML foundation'), server-rendered semantic HTML report (which also powers print), streaming as enhancement with polling fallback, self-hosted fonts, no bleeding-edge CSS without fallbacks.

Five verified editorial references compatible with the 17A serif/sans system: The Markup (Ivar Display serif + Messina Sans + Roboto Mono — the aesthetic north star), The Marshall Project (Miller serif + Acumin Pro), Vital City (civic data explorers inside an editorial frame — the mission analog), Works in Progress (Editor serif, warm off-white #fff7f4 ground — the warm-neutral color model), ProPublica (tokenized hed/sans/serif system, 'How we did this' methodology boxes → transparency panels).

Borrow Jobscan's loop mechanics: publish the count of checks run ('30+ checks'), group findings by category, and support re-scan after the user gets vendor answers — turning a one-shot verdict into a repeatable triage workflow.
